doc.title: Bob Rosengarden interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 6, 1996

title: The shared drum cases at the recording studios
summary: Studio drummers shared locked drum cases left at studios so they could go straight from the Cavett show to sessions.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: From a logistical standpoint, how did you drummers manage that?

Oh, a whole bunch of us who did recording sessions, finally got smart. I don’t know who thought of the idea, Don Lamond was a very busy drummer in those days, there was a guy who has since died, Terry Snyder who was doing the Como show. Very good drummer. Eddie Shaughnessy. Oh there were a whole bunch of us. So what we did is we would get a drum case, each would contribute a drum case with snare drum and stands and sticks and brushes and cymbals. Since I did a lot of Latin work, I would carry my bongos with me in like a little suitcase. And so in each studio, somebody, we got together and decided, okay, I’ll have my drum case at RCA Victor, 24th Street. You have yours at Columbia, 30th Street and the jingle houses and so forth, so there was always a drum case there and we had a combination lock with the same combination so that the strangers couldn’t come in and borrow things. And as a result, we’d finish the job, and on the Cavett show everything stayed the same, the set stayed the same. We’d finish, get off, grab a cab, go down to the session, walk in, open up the lock, take out the snare drum or whatever you needed and you know it was the best of all possible worlds. I mean I don’t think about it anymore, but now that we’re talking about it you know it was as good as it sounds.
